title: Banning AI in Schools While Embracing AI in Assessment for Accountability: A Bad Deal for Kids
author: Terry U.
summary: This essay argues that the 2026 wave of district-level AI bans in New York City, Los Angeles, and Chicago repeats the 2023 ChatGPT panic while ignoring a much larger and less visible use of AI already embedded in American schools: automated essay and test scoring for high-stakes accountability exams. The author traces how the rationale for banning classroom AI shifted between 2023 and 2026 from fears about cheating to fears about screen time and child development, even as teacher AI adoption nearly doubled in the interim. Its central move is to juxtapose the well-publicized instructional bans against the largely unexamined use of natural-language-processing engines to grade state tests in Texas, Louisiana, and elsewhere, arguing that students are simultaneously forbidden from using AI to help them think and subjected to AI they cannot see or contest when their work is judged. The piece concludes that policymakers are targeting the politically visible, low-cost intervention (banning classroom AI) while leaving the higher-stakes, budget-saving use of AI in assessment completely untouched.
points: The 2023 and 2026 AI bans in NYC, LA, and Chicago look like a rerun but are actually a second wave following a real embrace period in which teacher AI use nearly doubled (34% to 61%), showing the panic cycle is driven by shifting political anxieties, not new evidence of harm.

Texas's STAAR exam already has an automated scoring engine grading roughly 75% of constructed-response items, cutting the human-scoring workforce from 6,000 to under 2,000 -- a scale of AI dependence in high-stakes testing that dwarfs anything being debated in the classroom-use bans.

The rationale for banning student AI use has never been matched by an equivalent scrutiny of AI grading systems, because the former is politically visible and costless while unwinding the latter threatens real savings and entrenched accountability infrastructure.

Students face a double bind: barred from using AI to develop their own thinking, they are simultaneously graded by AI systems they cannot question, inverting the stated 'protect the children' logic driving the bans.
quotes: In 2026 Los Angeles Unified imposed its own moratorium on student generative-AI use on district devices, extending across all grades, citing parental concern about tech reliance and tying it to the board's screen-time restrictions. The same anxiety surfaced in Chicago in 2026 not by fiat but by referendum.

Strangely enough, after the 2023 ban, EdWeek's research center found teacher AI use nearly doubled from 34% in 2023 to 61% by 2025. NYC reversed its original ban in May 2023, months after imposing it.

Since 2024, the Texas Education Agency has used an automated scoring engine, built on the same natural-language-processing techniques underlying tools like ChatGPT, to grade roughly 75 percent of constructed-response items on the STAAR exam. The system cut the state's human-scoring workforce from 6,000 to fewer than 2,000 and saved $15-20 million a year.

Students are being denied access to AI in the one context where they could learn to control it in their own learning, writing, thinking at the exact moment the same institutions are deepening their reliance on AI in the one context where students have zero control: being judged by it.

The "protect children" rationale driving the bans targets low-stakes, visible use. Who is protecting the children during the high-stakes, invisible use? Denise Pope's decade of data showing flat cheating rates suggests the instructional ban isn't a response to a demonstrated harm, whereas the assessment system's harms are demonstrable and are not being banned.
Protecting kids from AI" and "protecting the budget with AI" are running on parallel tracks, and only one of them is getting headlines.
